blocks.content: In a similar fashion to the Wright-Castle estimator for the number of loci (LW Chapter 9), if we are willing to make the assumption of the exchangeable model (all loci are additive with the same effects and initial frequencies; Chapter 24), we can estimate a, n, and $ p_0 $ from data on selection limits. Under this model, Equation 25.1b gives the expected total response ($ R_c(\infty) $, which we will simply write here as $ R $) of $ 2na(1 - p_0) $, while the starting additive variance is $ 2na^2p_0(1 - p_0) $. Using these expressions yields Robertson's (1970a) result for the total response, scaled by the square root of the initial additive variance, as [[SEE_FORMULA:25.2a]]

Dudley (1977) noted that, in a divergence selection experiment (Chapter 18), Equation 25.2a yields the limit, $ R_{H} $, for response in the high direction, while [[SEE_FORMULA:25.2b]] yields the limit to response in the low direction. Taking the ratio of these two limits yields [[SEE_FORMULA:25.2c]]
Equation 25.2c rearranges to suggest an estimate of $ p_{0} $, with [[SEE_FORMULA:25.2d]]
Next, because $ R_H R_L = 4n^2 a^2 p_0 (1 - p_0) $, it follows that $ R_H R_L / \sigma_A^2 = 2n $, which suggests an estimator for the number of loci [[SEE_FORMULA:25.2e]]
Finally, a little algebra recovers an estimate of the allelic effect, namely, [[SEE_FORMULA:25.2f]]

These estimates of the genetic architecture of a trait should be regarded as extremely crude (at best), but they nonetheless provide potential insight. One of the many caveats in applying these results is that the selected populations must be at their respective limits, which can be hard to access. Operationally, the limits could be estimated from curve-fitting of the data, a topic that will be discussed shortly.
